messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur Vance was fifty-one when a sudden cardiac arrhythmia dropped him during a morning staff meeting at the high school he led for twelve years. He was rushed to the county hospital, where the emergency team’s rapid response left him with a lasting imprint of the burning antiseptic on his skin and the heavy, chemical tang of industrial alcohol swabs against his throat. The weeks that followed were a blur of intubation, chest compressions, and the relentless hum of life support. Because his survival depended entirely on those precise clinical environments, the antiseptic and alcohol odors became inextricably linked to his own mortality. Now, the sharp alcohol scent in the staff restroom or the sight of a nurse’s clipboard instantly pulls the trauma forward. That olfactory cue doesn’t merely remind him of the event; it forces the fragmented images of the ICU to surface against his will, and the sheer physiological terror of that moment quickly convinces him that his body can no longer be trusted. The conviction that his physiology was fundamentally unreliable reshaped how Arthur moved through the day. Because he was certain he could no longer rely on his own cardiovascular stability, he systematically withdrew from situations that might demand physical exertion or unexpected medical attention. He began rehearsing every faculty meeting script in his head long before he entered the building, and he stopped returning calls from his late wife’s siblings, claiming exhaustion. These rigid coping habits were his direct response to the negative self-evaluations that took hold; he believed only through extreme control and withdrawal could he prevent another collapse. Yet, his isolation and constant internal monologues soon fed back into his trauma processing. The more he rehearsed conversations and cut off his support network, the less grounded he felt, which in turn made the hospital smells and medical procedures in the school clinic trigger a fresh wave of dread. Arthur’s memory quality dictated his daily reality. When he attempted to deliberately access the hospital timeline, he found the narrative fragmented and impossible to reconstruct, a gap that deepened his suspicion that his mind was failing him. This deliberate retrieval failure, combined with moments when the full emotional intensity of the arrest flooded his chest without any clear image, solidified his belief that he had become an unrecognisable version of himself. The very triggers that sparked these memories also dictated his daily routines; because the alcohol wipes and examination tables provoked such visceral disorientation, he instituted a strict policy of avoiding any district health screenings and delegated all medical-related parent communications. His maladaptive avoidance patterns, in turn, starved his cognitive processing of corrective evidence, which allowed his negative appraisals to fester and sharpen. When his self-evaluations grew sufficiently severe, they acted as a cognitive filter, pulling the most terrifying fragments of his medical trauma to the forefront of his awareness whenever he was alone. The cycle tightened relentlessly across the following months. Arthur’s negative appraisals of his own fragility directly heightened his hypervigilance, causing him to scan every corridor for the scent of antiseptic long before his body could register it. Simultaneously, the bodily reenactment that accompanied his intrusive memories—the phantom stiffness of his hospital gown and the remembered pressure of the ventilator—drove him to further isolate completely, refusing even casual lunches with former colleagues. These compounding strategies only reinforced his conviction that he was fundamentally broken. The administrative duties that once anchored his identity now felt like minefields, forcing him to pace the linoleum hallways and check his pulse beneath his collar before entering any meeting. At fifty-two, Arthur Vance finally attended an intake session, hoping for relief from the suffocating loop, but terrified that seeking care would mean returning to the very medical cues that had once nearly killed him.
